title: Design product search for an online store
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, inverted index, facets, indexing pipeline, autocomplete, ranking.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Product search lets a shopper type "red running shoes" and get a ranked, filterable list of products in under a few hundred milliseconds. Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy and Shopify stores all do this. The hard parts are text relevance, filters (facets such as brand, price, size) and keeping the index in sync with a catalog that changes every second (price, stock).

Functional requirements

  • Free-text search with typo tolerance and synonyms ("sneakers" = "shoes").
  • Filters and facets (brand, price range, rating, in-stock) with counts.
  • Sorting: relevance, price, rating, newest. Pagination.
  • Autocomplete suggestions while typing.
  • Product changes (new item, price change, out of stock) appear in search within seconds to a minute.

Non-functional requirements

  • Search p99 under 200 ms; autocomplete p99 under 50 ms.
  • Availability 99.95%. Search may be slightly stale (eventual consistency), but never show wrong price at checkout (checkout re-reads the source of truth).
  • Scale: 50M products, 20k search QPS at peak.

Decision gravity. Choose a dedicated search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr, or Algolia/Typesense as a service) instead of SQL LIKE '%shoe%'. LIKE with a leading wildcard scans every row; at 50M rows it takes seconds. The inverted index is the one-way-ish door: the catalog stays in the primary DB, and the search index is a derived copy you can always rebuild, which keeps the decision reversible.

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a textbook: instead of reading every page for "photosynthesis", you look up the word and get page numbers.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing to search in the main SQL database with LIKE.
  • Not asking whether price and stock must be real time in search (usually no, only at checkout).
  • Forgetting facets and sort, which drive most of the real complexity.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
GET /v1/search?q=red+running+shoes&brand=nike,adidas&priceMin=2000&priceMax=8000
    &inStock=true&sort=relevance&pageSize=24&cursor=eyJzY29yZSI6My4yLCJpZCI6OTl9

200 OK
{ "total": 1842,
  "items": [ { "id": "p_9981", "title": "Nike Revolution 6 Running Shoes",
               "price": 3495, "currency": "INR", "rating": 4.4, "inStock": true,
               "imageUrl": "https://cdn.shop.com/p_9981.jpg" } ],
  "facets": { "brand": [ {"value":"nike","count":412}, {"value":"adidas","count":288} ],
              "price":  [ {"from":0,"to":2000,"count":120}, {"from":2000,"to":5000,"count":900} ] },
  "nextCursor": "eyJzY29yZSI6Mi45LCJpZCI6MTAwfQ==",
  "queryId": "q_7f3a" }
GET /v1/suggest?q=runn&limit=8
200 { "suggestions": ["running shoes", "running shorts", "runner's watch"] }
POST /v1/internal/products/p_9981      // catalog service publishes change events
{ "title": "...", "price": 3295, "inStock": false, "version": 417 }
202 Accepted

Pagination: use a cursor (search_after in Elasticsearch: the sort values of the last item) rather than from=10000&size=24. Deep offset paging makes every shard sort from+size hits and gets slow past about 10,000 (Elasticsearch caps it at index.max_result_window = 10,000 by default).

Industry example. Elasticsearch's _search with search_after; Algolia and Typesense expose nearly the same query-plus-facets shape.

Everyday analogy. A librarian who hands you one tray of books at a time and bookmarks where you stopped.

Common interview traps.

  • Offset pagination on huge result sets.
  • Returning full product documents instead of the small card fields.
  • No queryId returned, so click-through data cannot be tied back to a query for ranking.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 50M products, 20k peak search QPS, 5k peak autocomplete QPS per "typing burst".

Quantity Calculation Result
Index doc size title+desc+attrs ~2 KB text, plus index overhead ~3 KB
Index size 50M x 3 KB ~150 GB (x2 with 1 replica = 300 GB)
Shards target 20-40 GB per shard ~6 primary shards, 12 total
Search QPS per node one data node ~ 500-1,500 simple queries/s 20k QPS needs ~20-40 data nodes with replicas
Autocomplete 1 keystroke per ~150 ms; debounce to 1 per 300 ms big traffic multiplier, cache heavily
Update rate 5% of catalog changes daily = 2.5M updates/day ~30/s average, bursts of thousands/s during sales
Bandwidth 20k QPS x 15 KB response ~300 MB/s outbound

Reads dominate the shape: index size is modest (hundreds of GB), the pain is query CPU and the facet aggregations.

Industry example. Etsy and Wayfair run Elasticsearch/Solr clusters of dozens to hundreds of nodes; Flipkart has described its own search stack on Solr/Elasticsearch with a separate ranking layer.

Everyday analogy. Counting how many shelves a warehouse needs before buying them.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing only storage, not query CPU.
  • Forgetting replicas double the storage.
  • Ignoring burst writes during a flash sale.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Two paths: an offline/near-real-time path that builds the index from the catalog, and an online path that answers queries.

Components:

  • Catalog DB (Postgres/MySQL/DynamoDB): the source of truth for products.
  • Change stream (Debezium CDC or app-published events into Kafka): every product change becomes an event with a monotonic version.
  • Indexer: consumes events, builds the search document, upserts into the index. Uses version as external versioning so a late old event never overwrites a newer one.
  • Search cluster: sharded inverted index, 6 primary shards x 2 replicas.
  • Query understanding: spell correction, synonyms, stemming, category prediction ("nike" is a brand).
  • Ranker: first pass BM25 in the engine, second pass re-rank the top 200 with a learning-to-rank model using clicks, price, availability.
  • Result cache: Redis, key = hash(normalized query + filters + page), TTL 60 s for popular queries.

Decision gravity: derived index fed by events. Why: the DB stays authoritative, the index can be rebuilt from scratch (reindex into a new index and swap an alias, zero downtime). Alternative: dual-write from the app to DB and index; it drifts when one write fails. Alternative: nightly full batch only; stale for hours. It breaks if the event stream loses messages, so run a periodic reconcile job comparing counts and checksums. Fully reversible.

Decision gravity: shard count. The number of primary shards is fixed at index creation in Elasticsearch; changing it means reindexing. Overshard slightly (and use rollover/alias swaps) so the one-way door can still be walked through later.

Industry examples. Amazon and Shopify feed search from catalog change streams; LinkedIn built its own engine (Galene) on a similar pattern.

Everyday analogy. A shop's printed catalog is reprinted from the master ledger whenever pages change; nobody edits the printed catalog by hand.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing to DB and index in the same request without a recovery story.
  • Updating index on every stock tick (use batching/debounce of 1-5 s).
  • No plan for reindexing with zero downtime (alias swap).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
The inverted index and relevance

An inverted index maps each token to a list of document IDs (postings). "red" -> [3, 17, 99]; "shoes" -> [17, 42, 99]. A query intersects the lists. Scoring uses BM25: rarer words weigh more, repeated words saturate, long fields are normalised.

Boost the title field 3x over description; use multi_match with type: best_fields. Typos use fuzziness AUTO (edit distance 1 for 3-5 chars, 2 for more). Decision gravity: analyzers are baked into the index at write time; changing the stemmer means a full reindex, so treat the analyzer as a one-way door and test it on real queries first.

Filters and facets

Filters (brand = nike) go in the filter context: no scoring, cached bitsets, fast. Facet counts use aggregations (terms on a keyword field with doc values). Heavy facets on high-cardinality fields (seller ID) are slow; limit to top 10 and approximate.

Keeping the index fresh

Partition Kafka by productId so events for one product stay ordered. Index with version_type=external: an event with version lower than the stored one is rejected. Inventory flips (out of stock) use partial update. Refresh interval default is 1 s; for bulk reindex set it to -1 and restore afterwards.

Decision gravity: eventual consistency in search is acceptable because checkout re-validates price and stock from the source of truth. If you promised exactness you would pay with slower writes and no cache.

Autocomplete

Use a completion suggester (FST in memory) or an edge_ngram field; rank suggestions by query popularity from logs. Cache the top prefixes in Redis and in the CDN (prefixes of 1-3 characters cover the huge majority of traffic). Client debounces 150-300 ms and cancels in-flight requests.

Scatter-gather and tail latency

Each query goes to every shard (scatter), each returns its top N, the coordinator merges (gather). Latency is the slowest shard. Mitigation: replicas with adaptive replica selection, a per-query timeout of 150 ms returning partial results, and avoiding giant size values.

Ranking beyond text

Top 200 from BM25 are re-ranked with features: click-through rate, conversion, price vs category median, delivery speed, in-stock. Log impressions and clicks (using queryId) to Kafka to train the model offline. Hide out-of-stock items rather than deleting them (cheap, reversible).

Production incident patterns. (1) Heap pressure from a facet on a high-cardinality field: symptom is GC pauses and rising p99; metric: JVM old-gen usage over 75%. (2) A bulk reindex starves live queries: throttle indexing and give it a separate node group. (3) Indexer lag after a flash sale: watch Kafka consumer lag, scale workers.

Industry examples. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch at Etsy, Wayfair; Algolia and Typesense for smaller shops; Amazon A9 for its own ranking.

Everyday analogy. A reader who first flips to the index, then asks the shop assistant to sort the shortlist by what other customers liked.

Common interview traps.

  • Using sorting by price over the whole index without a filter (huge memory).
  • Treating autocomplete as the same traffic as search.
  • Forgetting that analyzer changes require reindexing.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• You separate the source of truth from the derived search index, and explain how they sync (CDC/Kafka, versions, reconcile).
  • You can explain an inverted index, BM25 and filters vs scoring in one minute.
  • Sensible shard and replica math from the estimates.
  • Cursor pagination, caching of hot queries, and tail-latency handling.
  • Freshness vs correctness: eventual search, strong at checkout.
  • Awareness of one-way doors (shard count, analyzers) and zero-downtime reindex via alias swap.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Use a dedicated search engine with an inverted index; SQL LIKE does not scale.
  • Catalog DB is the truth; events (CDC to Kafka) feed idempotent, versioned indexing.
  • ~150 GB index, ~6 primary shards with replicas; QPS drives node count.
  • Two-stage ranking: BM25 then ML re-rank of the top few hundred.
  • Filters are cached and unscored; facets are aggregations, limit cardinality.
  • Cursor pagination, result cache with short TTL, autocomplete served from prefix caches.
  • Analyzer and shard count are hard to change; reindex through aliases.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't we just search products with WHERE title LIKE '%shoe%' in the main database? What does a search engine do differently?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand the data structure behind search, not only tool names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A leading-wildcard LIKE cannot use a normal B-tree index, so the database scans every row; at 50M products that takes seconds and burns the primary's CPU. A search engine builds an inverted index: for each token it keeps a list of document IDs. A query looks up the tokens and intersects the lists, so cost depends on matches, not on catalog size. It also scores by relevance (BM25), handles typos, synonyms and facets. The catalog stays in the primary DB; the index is a derived copy I can rebuild.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
doc 3: "red running shoes"      red   -> [3, 17, 99]
doc 17: "red shoes sale"       shoes -> [3, 17, 42, 99]
                               query "red shoes" = [3,17,99] AND [3,17,42,99] = [3,17,99]
  • Text goes through an analysis chain: lowercase, tokenize, stem, synonyms. The same chain runs at index and query time.
  • BM25: rarer terms weigh more, repeated terms saturate, long fields are normalised. A title match is boosted over a description match.
  • Keeping the DB as the source of truth and the index as a derived store means a broken index is a rebuild, not data loss.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Proposing LIKE or a SQL full-text index for 50M products with facets and 20k QPS.
  • Treating the search index as the primary store.
  • Forgetting that analysis rules are baked in at write time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Postgres full text search solve this? -> It can for small catalogs; at this scale facets, relevance tuning and horizontal scaling favour a dedicated engine.
  2. How does "sneakers" match "shoes"? -> Synonym filter in the analysis chain.
  3. What does it cost? -> Extra storage (about 150 GB for 50M products at ~3 KB), an indexing pipeline, and eventual consistency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer names Elasticsearch. The senior answer explains postings lists, the derived-copy principle and rebuildability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that ran LIKE search on the orders DB saw checkout latency rise every time a campaign sent users to search.

questions.contextHtml: "Design product search for our store." No numbers, no description of what is searchable. The business owner mentions "price and stock must always be right".
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you decide about consistency?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts "always right" literally and designs synchronous writes to the index, or designs nothing until given numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Catalog size and change rate (50M products, 5% a day)? Peak search QPS? Which filters and sorts matter (brand, price, size, in-stock)? Typo tolerance and synonyms? How fresh must changes be: seconds or a minute? Is "always right" about search results, or about checkout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. I'd propose: search is eventually consistent (seconds to a minute), checkout re-reads price and stock from the source of truth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The cheap, safe split is search for discovery, DB for commitment. A user seeing a price that is 30 s old is acceptable if checkout shows the real one.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ask what happens today when a price differs between list and checkout; check refund and complaint data to gauge tolerance.
  5. Root cause: n/a. "Always right" usually means "never charge a wrong amount", which is solved at checkout.
  6. Fix: Design: catalog DB plus change stream into an index, versioned updates, hide out-of-stock quickly (partial update), checkout revalidation.
  7. Prevention: Metrics on index lag and a reconcile job so staleness is bounded and visible.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not promise real-time exactness in search; it costs slower writes and disables caching for little benefit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if legal requires prices to be exact on the list page? -> Fetch live price by product ID for the 24 results from a cache or pricing service after search, rather than indexing price as truth.
  • What about flash sales? -> Allow bursts of thousands of updates/s through batching and a short debounce.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shop wrote to the DB and index in one request. When the index was down for a minute, product edits failed. Moving to events decoupled them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Starts building without questions, or promises real-time exactness.
  • Hire: Asks scale, filters, freshness and separates search from checkout truth.
  • Strong hire: Frames consistency as a product decision and names reconcile and lag metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a query like "red running shoes" with brand and price filters, plus facet counts, is executed. Why are filters different from the text match?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most real search complexity is facets and filters, and many candidates only describe text matching.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The text part is scored (BM25 on title and description with boosts). Filters like brand = nike and a price range go into a filter context: they don't affect the score, so the engine can cache their result as a bitset and apply it quickly. Facet counts are aggregations over the matching documents, usually on keyword fields with doc values. High-cardinality facets, like seller ID, are expensive, so I limit them to the top N or approximate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Query -> scored text match (BM25) --\
Query -> cached filter bitsets -------> merge hits -> facet aggregation -> response
  • Filters are binary: a doc matches or not. The engine keeps a per-segment bitset it can reuse across queries.
  • Aggregations on terms of a keyword field use doc values (column-oriented, on disk and page cache).
  • Facet counts should be computed over the result set with the other filters applied but without the filter of the facet itself, so the UI can show "adidas (288)" while nike is selected. This is called multi-select facet logic.
  • In a sharded index each shard computes its counts and the coordinator merges; counts for terms can be approximate when you limit top N per shard.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting filters in a scoring clause, losing caching and distorting relevance.
  • Faceting on seller ID or free-text fields, which blows up heap.
  • Sorting by price across the whole index without a filter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are terms facet counts approximate? -> Each shard returns its top-N terms; a term that is mid-ranked on all shards can be missed.
  2. How do you speed up price buckets? -> Precomputed ranges or a range aggregation on a numeric field.
  3. How do you keep p99 flat? -> Bound facet size, limit fields, cache hot queries for 60 s, and a query timeout returning partial results.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "filter by brand". The senior answer separates scoring from filtering, knows facets are aggregations with cardinality cost, and names multi-select semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An aggregation on a high-cardinality field pushed JVM old-gen over 75% and caused GC pauses across the cluster.

questions.contextHtml:
A bot and some real users scroll deep into results. The API is GET /v1/search?q=shoes&from=24000&size=24. Logs:

ERROR  Result window is too large, from + size must be less than or equal to: [10000]
       but was [24024]. See the scroll api for a more efficient way to request large data sets.
search p99: 180 ms -> 2.4 s during the bot's crawl, data nodes CPU 85%

Customers also report that page 3 sometimes repeats items from page 2 when prices change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise max_result_window", which moves the cost to every shard and heap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do real users need page 1000? Is deep paging a user or a bot behaviour? Is the sort order stable (a tie-breaker)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap pages at about 10,000 results, rate-limit the bot by IP and token, and return a friendly "refine your search" response.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Offset paging makes each shard sort from + size hits, then the coordinator merges them: cost grows with depth and shard count. Duplicates on page 3 come from changing sort values (price changed) or missing a tie-breaker on equal scores.
  4. How I'd verify each: Profile the slow query, check shard-level took, and replay the same query with a stable sort.
  5. Root cause: Offset pagination over a mutable, scored result set.
  6. Fix: Cursor pagination with search_after: the cursor encodes the last item's sort values plus a unique tie-breaker (such as product id). For consistent browsing use a point-in-time reader (PIT) where supported (verify the exact API in your engine version) or accept slight drift. Return nextCursor.
  7. Prevention: Maximum page size, rate limits, an alert on queries with a large from, tests for cursor stability.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Cursors do not allow jumping to page 40; I accept that, since users refine rather than jump. I would not use the scroll API for user-facing requests; it is meant for batch exports.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sort by relevance score? -> Cursor includes the score and id; scores can shift when the index changes, so use PIT for stability.
  • Mobile infinite scroll? -> Cursor fits naturally.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A crawler requested page 5,000 of a very broad query every minute. Offset paging on 12 shards doubled node CPU until a cursor and a page cap ended it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises the window limit.
  • Hire: Cursor with search_after, caps and tie-breaker.
  • Strong hire: Mentions PIT, bot control and why deep paging is a product smell.

questions.contextHtml: The business is acquiring a competitor: the catalog goes from 50M to 100M products and peak search QPS from 20k to 40k. Documents average 3 KB indexed. Target shard size 20-40 GB, one replica. A previous load test showed that a set of nodes holding one full copy of the index (every primary shard on its own node) sustained about 4k QPS at p99 under 200 ms. That number is an assumption from the test and should be re-measured.
questions.promptHtml: Size the cluster and say what you'd double-check.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Sizes only storage ("600 GB, so 3 nodes") and ignores query CPU, replicas and scatter-gather.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 40k QPS peak or average? Cache hit ratio for popular queries? Same query mix (facets, sorts)? Is peak driven by a sale?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (planning).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Storage is the easy part; QPS and aggregation CPU decide node count.
  4. How I'd verify each: Index size = 100M x 3 KB = 300 GB; with 1 replica 600 GB. At 30 GB per shard: 10 primaries, 20 shard copies. Query side: each search touches every primary shard, so one copy of the index (10 nodes) handles about 4k QPS. 40k QPS plus 30% headroom is about 52k QPS, so about 13 copies, roughly 130 data nodes. A result cache for hot queries (60 s TTL) at, say, a 40% hit ratio cuts that to about 8 copies. I'd benchmark with real queries before committing.
  5. Root cause: n/a. Shard count multiplies per-query work, so fewer, bigger shards (up to the size target) help.
  6. Fix: 10 primaries, replicas set by throughput not durability, separate coordinating nodes, result cache, autocomplete on its own small cluster.
  7. Prevention: Load test every quarter with replayed production traffic, watch per-shard latency and heap, autoscale replicas ahead of sales.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not oversize shard count (many tiny shards raise fan-out cost). But shard count is fixed at creation, so I'd leave a little room (reindex via alias swap if I'm wrong).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if storage doubles but QPS stays? -> More primaries, but the per-query fan-out also grows; consider routing or splitting by category.
  • Bandwidth? -> 40k QPS x 15 KB = 600 MB/s outbound.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added shards to fix slowness and made it worse: every query now touched more shards, so tail latency rose. Adding replicas fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Storage-only sizing.
  • Hire: Shard count from size, replicas from QPS, shows arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: Notes scatter-gather cost, cache, benchmarks and flags assumptions.

questions.contextHtml:
After a Kafka broker outage and recovery, customers report items showing "in stock" in search but sold out at checkout, and some prices are old. Metrics:

indexer consumer lag: 0 (recovered)      search p99: 120 ms (normal)
index doc count: 50,012,340              catalog rows: 50,016,905
product p_9981: DB version 417 price 3295 / index version 412 price 3495
indexer log: 4,100 events rejected "version conflict" in last hour
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the drift and explain how you repair and prevent it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reindex everything now", which loads the cluster and doesn't explain how it got out of sync.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did events get lost (retention, topic recreated) or only reordered? Is the producer publishing from CDC or the app? Are partitions keyed by productId?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hide out-of-stock items in the API response by a quick check against inventory for the visible results; this limits wrong "in stock" claims. Scale indexer workers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Events dropped during the outage (producer retries exhausted, or offsets reset), leaving the index behind. (b) Out-of-order events, which version conflicts reject correctly. (c) Indexer bug on partial updates. The lag being 0 is a red herring: it says the consumer caught up, not that nothing was lost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare doc counts and per-shard checksums between DB and index; query the 4,100 conflicts and see whether they are legitimately old; check topic retention and offset history; diff a sample of 10k products.
  5. Root cause: Lost events during the outage with no reconcile job to detect it. Conflicts themselves are fine; the version check protects newer data.
  6. Fix: Short-term: re-emit events for the time window from the DB (CDC snapshot or a query on updated_at >= outage start) and let versioned upserts make it idempotent. Long-term: a periodic reconcile comparing counts and checksums by range, plus a nightly full diff.
  7. Prevention: Alert on |DB count - index count|, freshness of the newest indexed update, consumer lag, DLQ size. Outbox pattern or CDC to avoid dual writes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not do a blind full reindex during peak; it starves live queries. I would not remove version checks to "fix" conflicts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would exactly-once help? -> The effect is achieved by idempotent versioned upserts; chasing exactly-once delivery adds cost.
  • How do you rebuild fully with zero downtime? -> Build a new index with refresh disabled, swap the alias, keep the old for rollback.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A topic was recreated during maintenance and ten minutes of price changes vanished. A reconcile job that nobody had thought necessary found it within the hour afterwards.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reindex everything immediately.
  • Hire: Finds lost events vs version conflicts, replays the window.
  • Strong hire: Reconcile job, alerts, outbox/CDC, and understands why lag 0 proves nothing.

questions.contextHtml: Search quality review says "running" does not match "run", and the team wants a better stemmer plus a synonym list. The index is 150 GB in 6 primary shards, serving 20k QPS. The same release should also move to 12 shards because shards are now 25 GB at 100M documents planned. A sale starts in 3 weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How do you ship this without downtime or relevance regressions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Update the mapping in place" (not allowed for analyzers on existing fields) or "take the site down at night".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I afford 2x index storage temporarily? What is the freshness SLA during migration (updates must keep flowing)? How do we measure relevance (click-through, judged queries)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a. I treat both the analyzer and shard count as one-way doors for the old index, but the swap itself is reversible if I keep the old index.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: relevance regressions, load from reindexing, missing updates made during the build, a cutover mistake.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay a sample of production queries against old and new indices and compare top-10 overlap and offline metrics; shadow traffic; canary.
  5. Root cause: Analyzers are applied at index time, so existing documents must be rewritten.
  6. Fix: Create products_v2 with new settings and 12 shards. Set refresh_interval = -1 and replicas 0 during the bulk load, throttle on a separate node group, then restore. Dual-feed: the live indexer writes to both indices (or replay events from a saved offset) so updates during the build are not lost. Verify counts and checksums, run shadow queries, canary 5% via the alias, then flip the alias products to v2. Keep v1 for a week for rollback.
  7. Prevention: Index and mapping in version control, automated relevance test set, runbook for alias swap.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not reindex during the sale; I'd finish at least a week before. I would not let the bulk job share nodes with live search.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the new stemmer lowers conversion? -> Roll the alias back; that is why v1 stays.
  • Can I use the reindex API from v1? -> It works but is slow for 150 GB and reads the source; rebuilding from the catalog DB through the same indexer code gives fresher data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team changed a synonym list live and "jeans" started matching "genes" products in a different category. Offline judged queries would have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: In-place change or downtime.
  • Hire: New index, alias swap, dual updates.
  • Strong hire: Shadow/canary with relevance metrics, throttling, rollback and timing around the sale.

questions.contextHtml:
During an afternoon, search p99 climbs from 180 ms to 4 s. Data nodes show:

node-7  jvm old gen 91%   gc pause 3.8 s   search rejected 1,204
node-3  jvm old gen 88%   gc pause 2.9 s
bulk indexing: running since 13:00 (nightly feed rerun by a seller)  cpu 40%
new dashboard widget: facet "seller" (terms agg size 10000) enabled at 12:40

Traffic is normal at 18k QPS.
questions.promptHtml: What is the cause and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the bulk indexing (a plausible red herring) and adds nodes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the last hour (deploys, features, feeds)? Which queries are slow (any, or only those with the seller facet)? Is the problem on all nodes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the seller facet via the feature flag, apply a query timeout (150 ms partial results), reject or throttle the bulk feed; circuit-break expensive aggregations.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A terms aggregation with size 10000 on a high-cardinality field consumes heap per shard and coordinator. (b) Bulk indexing competes for CPU and segment merges. (c) Fielddata or caches. (d) Traffic growth (ruled out: QPS is normal).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare timings with and without the facet using the slow log; check node stats for fielddata and request-breaker trips, hot threads; correlate timeline: 12:40 facet versus 13:00 bulk. Latency rose after 12:40 before the bulk started (verify from the graph).
  5. Root cause: The new high-cardinality facet exhausted heap, causing long GC pauses and rejections. Bulk load is secondary load.
  6. Fix: Limit facets to the top 10 with approximation, use the seller filter instead of a seller facet, and set circuit-breaker limits. Give bulk indexing its own node group and throttle it.
  7. Prevention: Query review for new aggregations, load test with facets, alert on old-gen over 75% and GC pause time, rate limit seller feeds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not simply add heap; bigger heaps mean longer GC pauses. I would not restart nodes in a rolling fashion during the problem; it shifts load to the remaining nodes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the facet is a business requirement? -> Precompute seller counts offline or search sellers in a separate small index.
  • What about scatter-gather tail? -> Adaptive replica selection and a per-query timeout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An engineer tested a new facet on a 1M-doc staging index and it looked fine. In production, 50M docs and 400k sellers made the coordinator allocate large per-request structures.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds nodes or blames bulk indexing only.
  • Hire: Spots the aggregation, disables it, isolates bulk.
  • Strong hire: Uses timeline correlation, breakers, a review gate and load tests with production cardinality.
